definition: Terrestrial fiber optic cable within a country: national and regional backbone, middle mile and backhaul, metropolitan rings, fiber to the home or premises, optical ground wire on power transmission lines (OPGW), dark fiber, ducts and conduit, and the trenching, poles, rights of way and civil works that carry them, including policy, regulation and technical assistance about them (right-of-way rules, infrastructure sharing, dig-once). Fiber connecting named schools, health facilities, government offices or communities at the last mile is access and connectivity; cross-border links are international connectivity.

Mobile and other ground-based wireless networks and the coverage they carry: mobile operators' radio access networks, base stations, towers and masts, 2G to 5G rollout, fixed wireless access, microwave links, terrestrial broadcast transmission, the passive site infrastructure of power, shelter and grounding, and spectrum and the policy, regulation and technical assistance about these networks (spectrum assignment, tower sharing, coverage obligations). Wireless links to named schools, health facilities, government offices or communities at the last mile are access and connectivity.

Satellite communications: ground stations and teleports, VSAT and other user terminals, capacity bought from low-earth-orbit, medium-earth-orbit or geostationary operators, satellite links used as backbone, backhaul or for remote and island sites, and the licensing, landing rights and technical assistance about them. Satellite links to named schools, health facilities, government offices or communities at the last mile are access and connectivity; satellite imagery and earth observation are geospatial data infrastructure.

A country's links to the rest of the world: submarine fiber optic systems (undersea cable, landing stations, branching units, beach manholes, marine route survey, cable laying and repair), cross-border terrestrial links, international gateways, the international bandwidth capacity these carry, and the policy, regulation and technical assistance about them (landing station access, open access, regional connectivity agreements).

Facilities and services that host, store, process and exchange data: data centres, server rooms, colocation space, government, sovereign and commercial cloud services, hosting migration, high-performance and AI computing capacity, internet exchange points (IXPs), the power and cooling equipment of these facilities, backup and secondary sites, the disaster recovery arrangements and business continuity of the systems they host, and the policy and technical assistance about them (cloud policy, data centre strategy). The systems hosted there (applications, registries, services) are not this unless the passage is about where or how they are hosted.

Networks that link public institutions to each other and to shared services: government wide-area networks (GovNet and similar), government virtual private networks, research and education networks (NRENs), school and education networks, health-sector networks, network operations centres, institutional local area networks, shared email, voice and unified communications services, and the policy and technical assistance to plan and manage them. The shared network stays here even when its members are schools, universities, hospitals or research institutions; the last-mile link that first connects a named unconnected school, health facility, office or community is access and connectivity.

Protection of digital systems and data as an activity of its own: security operations centres, computer emergency response teams, incident response, threat monitoring, cryptographic controls, network and application security, security audits and testing, and cybersecurity strategy, legislation, standards and capacity. A system's own security features mentioned in passing are that system, not this; personal data protection is digital public infrastructure.

Shared foundational digital systems used across the public sector and economy at population scale: digital identity and unique identification, civil registration and vital statistics, interoperable digital payment systems (national switches, fast payment systems, government-to-person payment rails), data exchange and interoperability layers, digital signatures and trust services, digital and verifiable credentials and the trust frameworks and public key infrastructure that issue and verify them, and personal data protection, consent and data governance, including the policy, regulation and technical assistance about them. Sector registries (social, land and cadastre, credit, collateral, business), applications, e-services and portals built on these are digital systems and applications, not this.

asset_name: Early warning and emergency communication systems
definition: Digital systems that detect, forecast and communicate hazards and emergencies: early warning systems, hydrological, meteorological, seismic and other hazard monitoring networks and sensors, forecasting systems, alerting and broadcast to the public (SMS, cell broadcast, sirens, radio and television alerts), emergency call and dispatch platforms, dedicated emergency radio networks (TETRA and similar) and emergency operations centres, and the policy and technical assistance about them. A risk assessment, screening or hazard map used to plan other infrastructure is not an asset; monitoring that runs a utility rather than warning the public is operational technology.

Connecting people and public institutions that lack connectivity, at the last mile: links to named schools, health facilities, government offices and communities by any technology (fiber, wireless or satellite), public access points and public Wi-Fi, community networks, user devices (computers, tablets, phones, school computer labs) and subscriptions provided to schools, health facilities, communities or beneficiaries so they can get online, and supply-side programmes that pay to connect them (universal service fund projects, subsidies or viability-gap payments to operators). Demand-side measures for users (affordability support, digital literacy and skills) are not this. Devices given to staff to operate a system are digital systems and applications. A backbone, backhaul, mobile, institutional or international network is not this unless the passage is about connecting those users or institutions at the last mile.

Digital monitoring and control of physical infrastructure in other sectors: SCADA and control systems for power, water, gas and transport; smart meters and advanced metering infrastructure; smart grid communications; intelligent transport systems (traffic management, tolling, signalling, fleet and vessel tracking); sensor and Internet of Things networks for utilities, agriculture, buildings and environment; and the field communications that link them. Monitoring that feeds hazard warnings to the public is early warning; software that analyses the data without controlling equipment is digital systems and applications.

Systems and equipment that capture, manage and share location data: spatial data infrastructure (SDI) platforms, geoportals, the systems and equipment of national mapping agencies, GIS platforms, satellite imagery and earth observation services, aerial and drone surveys, LiDAR, geodetic infrastructure (geodetic networks, datums, continuously operating reference stations or CORS), base mapping, and the policy and technical assistance about them. Land and cadastre registries that use this data are digital systems and applications; hazard maps made with it for risk assessment are not an asset.

Sector and government digital systems the project finances, builds or supports: information and management systems (health, education, public financial management, tax, customs, land and cadastre, justice, statistics, procurement, human resources), sector registries (social, credit, collateral, business), service platforms and portals, call-centre and case-management platforms, mobile and web applications, the software and data they are built from, and the workstations, tablets, handheld devices and other end-user equipment required to operate them. Shared foundational layers (identity, payment systems, data exchange) are digital public infrastructure, location data platforms are geospatial data infrastructure, and where systems are hosted is data infrastructure.
